title: functools: lru_cache, partial, reduce

glossary.definition: Caching a function's results by its arguments so repeat calls with the same inputs return instantly. `@lru_cache` does this automatically.

overview.why: Memoization is the difference between an O(2^n) and an O(n) solution — it's the backbone of top-down dynamic programming, which your DSA track leans on. partial and reduce round out a functional-style toolkit that shows up in real codebases.

why_learning_this: `@lru_cache` converts exponential recursive solutions into linear ones — the core trick behind top-down DP.
partial and reduce are common functional patterns you'll read in real code and use for callbacks and folds.

common_mistakes.title: Caching a function with unhashable arguments
common_mistakes.explanation: `lru_cache` keys the cache on the arguments, so they must be hashable. Calling an lru_cached function with a `list` or `dict` raises `TypeError: unhashable type`. Pass tuples/frozensets instead.

common_mistakes.title: Memoizing an impure function
common_mistakes.explanation: `lru_cache` returns the stored result for repeat args and never re-runs the body. If the function depends on time, randomness, or external state, you'll get stale answers. Only cache pure functions.

common_mistakes.title: Unbounded cache growth
common_mistakes.explanation: `maxsize=None` caches every distinct argument forever, which can leak memory for functions called with many unique inputs. Use a finite `maxsize` (default 128) when the input space is large.

recall_questions.q: How does `@lru_cache` change the time complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci, and why?
recall_questions.answer: From exponential O(2^n) to linear O(n). It caches each `fib(k)` the first time it's computed, so the overlapping subproblems are looked up instead of recomputed.

recall_questions.q: Why can't you call an `lru_cache`-decorated function with a list argument?
recall_questions.answer: The cache keys on the arguments, which must be hashable. Lists (and dicts/sets) are unhashable, so it raises TypeError. Use a tuple/frozenset instead.

practice_tasks.title: Memoize an expensive recursion
practice_tasks.prompt: Add `@lru_cache` to the recursive `count_paths` grid-walk function so repeated subproblems aren't recomputed, then print `count_paths(15, 15)` (which is far too slow without caching).

code_walkthrough.focus: fib.cache_info()  (hits show subproblems were reused, not recomputed)

understanding_checks.question: A developer decorates `def now(): return datetime.now()` with `@lru_cache`. Why does it always return the same time after the first call?
understanding_checks.answer: lru_cache stores the first result and returns it for every later call with the same (here, empty) arguments, never re-executing the body.
understanding_checks.why: Memoization assumes the function is pure — output depends only on arguments. `now()` depends on the clock (external state), so caching freezes it at the first value. Don't cache impure functions.

understanding_checks.question: Why does this raise a TypeError?
understanding_checks.answer: The argument `[1, 2, 3]` is a list, which is unhashable, and lru_cache must hash arguments to key the cache.
understanding_checks.why: lru_cache stores results keyed by arguments, requiring them to be hashable. A list can't be hashed; passing a tuple `(1, 2, 3)` would work.
